label: The Flat Torus Theorem
notes: Open by framing the chapter's promise: commuting semisimple isometries of a CAT(0) space force flat Euclidean subspaces to appear. We will meet the Flat Torus Theorem, the Splitting Theorem, and the Solvable Subgroup Theorem, and see how each constrains the groups that can act geometrically on non-positively curved spaces.

label: Semisimple Isometries and Min Sets
notes: Recall that an isometry is semisimple when its displacement function attains its infimum. Define the translation length and the min set as the locus where that infimum is realized. Stress that for a hyperbolic semisimple isometry the min set is a union of parallel axes, the raw material every later construction will exploit.

label: The Product Decomposition of Min Sets
notes: Present the key structural lemma: when an isometry is semisimple and hyperbolic, its min set splits isometrically as a product of a convex set with the real line. Emphasize that the line factor carries the translation and the convex factor records the transverse degrees of freedom. This product is what we iterate.

label: The Flat Torus Theorem
notes: State the theorem precisely: a free abelian group of rank n acting properly by semisimple isometries leaves invariant an isometrically embedded copy of Euclidean n-space, and acts on it cocompactly by translations. Underline each hypothesis, since dropping properness or semisimplicity breaks the conclusion in concrete ways we revisit later.

label: Building the Flat by Induction
notes: Walk through the induction on rank. A single generator gives an axis; the product splitting of its min set houses the remaining commuting generators, which act on the convex factor. Apply the inductive hypothesis there to obtain a flat of one lower dimension, then reassemble the line factor to lift it to full rank.

label: The Invariant Flat E^n
notes: Visualize the output: a genuine isometrically embedded Euclidean plane sitting inside the larger CAT(0) space, invariant under the whole group. The commuting translations generate a lattice acting on this flat. Insist that the embedding is isometric, not merely topological, so Euclidean geometry holds exactly on the flat.

label: The Flat Torus Quotient
notes: Explain how the lattice of translations yields the quotient. Because Z^n acts cocompactly by translations on E^n, the quotient is a compact flat n-torus, the geometric object that names the theorem. The fundamental domain is a parallelepiped whose side vectors are the translation vectors of a generating set.

label: The Splitting Theorem
notes: Introduce the Splitting Theorem: if a CAT(0) space contains a geodesic line whose two endpoint families are preserved, equivalently an invariant line, then the space splits isometrically as a product of the real line with a convex subspace. This is the engine behind the inductive step in the Flat Torus Theorem.

label: How an Axis Forces a Splitting
notes: Show the mechanism: parallel geodesic lines in a CAT(0) space bound flat strips, and the union of all lines parallel to a fixed one is convex and splits off a real factor. An invariant axis therefore produces a global product. Connect this directly back to the min set decomposition from slide three.

label: The Solvable Subgroup Theorem
notes: State the Solvable Subgroup Theorem: a solvable subgroup of a group acting properly cocompactly by isometries on a CAT(0) space is virtually abelian, and in fact finitely generated and acting on a flat. Highlight that this sharply limits which solvable groups can be CAT(0), ruling out many polycyclic examples.

label: Consequences for CAT(0) Groups
notes: Survey the structural payoff. Centralizers of hyperbolic elements split, polynomial distortion is forbidden, and abelian subgroups have bounded rank tied to the geometry. These corollaries turn the Flat Torus Theorem into a working toolkit for distinguishing CAT(0) groups from other classes of non-positively curved groups.

label: Summary and Outlook
notes: Recap the chain: semisimple commuting isometries to product min sets, to an invariant flat, to a flat torus quotient, to constraints on solvable subgroups. Preview that these flats reappear in the study of buildings and boundaries, and remind students that properness and semisimplicity were the load-bearing hypotheses throughout.
